tip.title: me levanto, me ducho
tip.body: Some routine verbs come with me in front: me levanto (I get up), me ducho (I shower), me acuesto (I go to bed). Literally "I get myself up". Others don't: desayuno (I have breakfast), trabajo, ceno (I have dinner). Add the time with a las …: me levanto a las siete.

tip.title: por la mañana, por la tarde, por la noche
tip.body: Use por la mañana (in the morning), por la tarde (in the afternoon / early evening) and por la noche (at night) for parts of the day. With a clock time it's de: a las ocho de la mañana, a las cinco de la tarde. Los fines de semana means "at weekends", and entre semana "during the week".

tip.title: hacer and tener que
tip.body: Lots of chores use hacer (to do / make): hago la compra (I do the shopping), hago la cama (I make the bed). To say what you have to do, use tengo que + infinitive: tengo que lavar la ropa. Some words change by region: fregar los platos (Spain) is lavar los platos in Latin America.

lessons.title: Reflexive verbs & the present
lessons.goal: Describe routines for yourself and others.

tip.title: Endings plus a little pronoun
tip.body: Regular verbs change their ending for each person. -ar: trabajo, trabajas, trabaja, trabajamos, trabajan. -er: como, comes, come, comemos, comen. -ir: vivo, vives, vive, vivimos, viven. Reflexive verbs add a pronoun before the verb: me levanto, te levantas, se levanta, nos levantamos, se levantan. A few change their stem: acostarse → me acuesto, despertarse → me despierto (but nos acostamos, nos despertamos).

story.intro: A radio presenter in Puebla, Mexico, interviews Don Ramón about his day as a baker.

lines.t: Don Ramón, usted es panadero. ¿A qué hora se levanta?

lines.name: Don Ramón
lines.t: Me levanto a las tres de la mañana. Me ducho, tomo un café y salgo de casa.
lines.n: I get up at three in the morning. I shower, have a coffee and leave home.

lines.name: Locutora
lines.t: ¿Y a qué hora se acuesta?

lines.name: Don Ramón
lines.t: Muy temprano, a las ocho y media. ¡Mi día empieza de noche!

culture.title: The siesta and the late timetable
culture.body: Many people imagine that everyone in Spain sleeps after lunch, but most working people in cities don't have time for a daily siesta: for many it's a weekend or holiday treat. What is real is the late timetable. In Spain lunch is often around 2 or 3 pm and dinner at 9 pm or later, and in smaller towns many shops close for a few hours in the afternoon. In Mexico, too, the main meal (la comida) is usually eaten in the afternoon, and dinner tends to be lighter. So if someone invites you a comer, they mean lunch, not dinner.

free.hint: Use Me levanto a las …, Me ducho, Desayuno …, Trabajo / Estudio …, Como a las …, Por la tarde …, Ceno …, Me acuesto a las ….
